title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every subarray directly versus a running prefix sum with a hash map.

blocks.text: Given an array nums and an integer k, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k. The array may contain negative numbers.

blocks.text: The single element subarray [0] sums to exactly 0, so with k equal to 0, the answer is 1.
It is worth asking why a sliding window, which works well for similar looking sum problems, does not apply here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If every number in nums were guaranteed non negative, growing and shrinking a sliding window would work, since the running sum would only ever move in one direction as the window changes.

Observation 2: Because negative numbers are allowed, growing the window does not always increase the sum, so a sliding window cannot reliably decide which direction to move, ruling it out entirely.

Observation 3: Two Sum already showed how to turn "does a matching earlier value exist" into an O(1) hash lookup instead of a nested scan. Here, the sum of a subarray from just after index i to index j equals the prefix sum up to j minus the prefix sum up to i, so a subarray summing to k ending at j exists whenever some earlier prefix sum equals the current prefix sum minus k.

Observation 4: Storing a running count of how many times each prefix sum value has occurred (not just whether it occurred, since it can repeat) turns that search into a single hash map lookup per position, confirmed by tracing nums equal to [1, 2, 3] with k equal to 3 through to the correct count, 2.

Recognizing a subarray sum as the difference between two prefix sums is what replaces an O(n squared) scan with a single pass hash map lookup, and it is exactly why negative numbers, which break the sliding window, are handled correctly here.
Check every contiguous subarray directly, keeping a running sum as the subarray grows, and count how many of those sums equal k.

items: For every starting index i, start a running sum at 0.
Extend the subarray one element at a time to every ending index j, adding nums[j] to the running sum.
Whenever the running sum equals k, increment the count.

codes.python:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = 0
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):                                      # every possible starting index
        running_sum = 0
        for j in range(i, n):                                 # extend the subarray one step at a time
            running_sum += nums[j]
            if running_sum == k:
                count += 1
    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3]
    k = 3
    print(subarray_sum(nums, k))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every starting index is tried, and for each one the subarray grows one element at a time, so every contiguous subarray is checked exactly once.
The running sum for a given start is simply extended rather than recomputed from scratch on each extension, keeping the inner loop itself linear.
This directly handles negative numbers correctly, since every subarray sum is computed explicitly rather than assumed to move in one direction.

blocks.text: Every contiguous subarray is directly summed and checked, so every matching subarray is guaranteed to be counted, including when negative numbers are present.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for every pair of start and end indices.
Space: O(1), only the running sum and count are kept.

Limitation: negative numbers rule out a sliding window shortcut (shrinking the window when the sum gets too large does not work if adding more elements could bring the sum back down), and the brute force does not exploit any structure in the cumulative sums to skip ahead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it recomputes and checks every subarray sum independently, even though many subarrays share the exact same starting prefix.

What the prefix sum identity fixes directly: any subarray sum from i plus 1 to j equals prefix[j] minus prefix[i], so a subarray ending at j sums to k exactly when prefix[i] equals prefix[j] minus k, for some earlier position i.

What Two Sum already proved about this kind of lookup: instead of scanning backward for that matching prefix[i], a hash map turns the search into a single O(1) average lookup.

The core idea: keep a running prefix sum, and a hash map counting how many times each prefix sum value has been seen so far, so every position can check for a match in constant time, seeding the map with prefix sum 0 occurring once to correctly count subarrays starting at index 0.

The sum of any subarray from index i plus 1 to j equals the prefix sum up to j minus the prefix sum up to i. So a subarray summing to k exists ending at position j whenever some earlier prefix sum equals the current prefix sum minus k. Keeping a running count of how many times each prefix sum value has occurred lets every position check for a match in constant time.
Keep a hash map from prefix sum value to how many times it has occurred, and for each position check how many earlier prefix sums equal the current prefix sum minus k.

blocks.caption: Optimized: a running prefix sum with a hash map of how often each sum has occurred

codes.python:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = 0
    prefix_sum = 0
    seen = {0: 1}                                           # an empty prefix (sum 0) has occurred once
    for num in nums:
        prefix_sum += num
        count += seen.get(prefix_sum - k, 0)                    # how many earlier prefixes complete a sum of k
        seen[prefix_sum] = seen.get(prefix_sum, 0) + 1
    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3]
    k = 3
    print(subarray_sum(nums, k))

blocks.text: This works because every earlier prefix sum equal to the current prefix sum minus k identifies exactly one valid subarray ending at the current position, so summing up how many times that specific value has already occurred, using the hash map's stored counts, correctly counts every matching subarray without ever re-scanning the array.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant time average map operations.
Space: O(n), for the map of prefix sum counts.

blocks.text: The prefix sum plus hash map pattern used here is the standard technique for "count subarrays matching a sum condition" problems, and the seeded entry for prefix sum 0 is what correctly counts subarrays that start from the very beginning of the array.

items: Attempting a sliding window approach, which only works when every number is guaranteed positive. With negative numbers allowed, shrinking or growing the window does not move the sum predictably in one direction.
Forgetting to seed the map with prefix sum 0 occurring once, which would silently undercount every subarray that starts at index 0.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "why not use a sliding window", think: negative numbers break the monotonic growth a sliding window depends on.
If the interviewer says "what does the hash map actually store", think: how many times each prefix sum value has occurred so far, not just whether it occurred.
If the interviewer says "what if all the numbers were guaranteed positive", think: a sliding window would then work, since the running sum could only grow as the window expands.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: running prefix sum combined with a hash map counting how many times each prefix sum value has occurred.

Core Idea: a subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums, so counting how many earlier prefixes equal the current prefix sum minus k turns subarray counting into a single hash map lookup per position.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach's hash map.
Most Important Observation: negative numbers make a sliding window unsafe, but they do not affect the prefix sum identity at all, which is why the hash map approach handles them cleanly.
Interview Difficulty: the prefix sum identity itself is a common trick; remembering to seed the map with prefix sum 0 occurring once is the detail most likely to be missed.
One line memory trick: count how many earlier prefixes equal the current prefix minus k.
